---
title: "Quiz: quadratic smoothing and total variation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Energy $E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q)$ with $\rho(d) = d^2/2$ (quadratic) or $\lvert d\rvert$ (TV).

---

**Q1.** Why is quadratic smoothing "just a linear system", while TV is not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Differentiate the energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $\rho(d) = d^2/2$ every derivative of $E$ is linear in $\mathbf x$: setting the gradient to zero gives $(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y$. With $\lvert d\rvert$ the derivative is $\pm1$ (and undefined at 0), so the optimality conditions are not linear; TV needs a special algorithm (in 1D an exact one).
:::

---

**Q2.** A noisy image has a sharp edge of height 100. Why does quadratic smoothing blur it, while TV keeps it sharp?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the prior cost of one jump with many small steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A quadratic prior charges $d^2$: one jump of 100 costs $\tfrac12 \cdot 10^4$, the same rise in 10 steps of 10 costs $\tfrac12 \cdot 1000$: ten times less. So it spreads the edge into a ramp. TV charges the total height (100) however it is spread, so nothing is gained by blurring and the data, which say "sharp", win.
:::

---

**Q3.** In what sense is quadratic smoothing a low-pass filter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the solution do to a wave $+1, -1, +1, \dots$, and to a constant?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a long signal it multiplies each frequency $\omega$ by $1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega))$: 1 for a constant, $1/(1 + 4\lambda)$ for the fastest oscillation. High frequencies (noise, but also the sharp part of edges) are damped, low ones pass.
:::

---

**Q4.** What are **staircasing** and **contrast loss** in TV denoising?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What shapes do TV solutions consist of?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
TV solutions are made of flat runs. A smooth ramp in noisy data is therefore turned into a series of flat steps (staircasing). Each run is pulled towards its neighbours by about $\lambda/\text{width}$, so small or narrow features (a thin bright line, a small spot) lose contrast and eventually vanish.
:::

---

**Q5.** When would you prefer the Huber penalty over TV?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Huber is quadratic for small differences.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the image has both smooth gradients and sharp edges. Huber treats small differences quadratically, so ramps stay smooth (no staircases), and large differences linearly, so edges are not blurred.
:::

---

**Q6.** Samples from the TV prior look like rough random walks, not like flat plateaus. Why then are TV estimates piecewise constant?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which single image does the estimate pick from the posterior?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The estimate is the **minimum** of the energy (the MAP), not a typical sample. The kink of $\lvert d\rvert$ at 0 makes "exactly equal neighbours" a common place for the minimum to sit, although typical samples almost never have equal neighbours. The look of the estimate is a property of the optimisation, not of what the prior believes images look like.
:::

---

**Q7.** How does the noise level enter the quadratic smoothing system?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Start from the posterior with noise standard deviation $\sigma_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The posterior energy is $\frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\sum(x_p - y_p)^2 + \frac{\lambda'}2\sum(x_p - x_q)^2$; multiplying by $\sigma_n^2$ gives our form with $\lambda = \lambda'\sigma_n^2$. More noise means a larger effective $\lambda$: the data are trusted less and the image is smoothed more.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Why does $(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y$ always have exactly one solution?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf x^\top(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \|\mathbf x\|^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 > 0$ for every $\mathbf x \ne 0$ (with $\lambda \ge 0$): the matrix is positive definite, hence invertible. Equivalently the energy is strictly convex.
:::
